title: The Naval Postgraduate School has a new high performance AI computing system from NVIDIA
article:

Vice provost for warfare studies and leader of the NPS AI Task Force at the Naval Postgraduate School
NVIDIA donated an advanced AI computing system to the Naval Postgraduate School (NPS) through the NPS Foundation, which installed it along with funding for complex research projects and operational problem-solving supporting the NPS-NVIDIA Cooperative Research and Development Agreement. The new platform gives NPS students and faculty access to frontier AI computing power and operates within the school’s existing infrastructure.

Terry Gerton It’s an exciting new development out there at the Naval Postgraduate School. You all have received an advanced AI computing system from NVIDIA. I will confess my lack of knowledge here, but I’m curious, what exactly came in the box? When you get an advanced AI computing system, what do you actually get?
Mike Owen So, the system we got, the Grace Blackwell 300 or GB300 from NVIDIA is a three rack supercomputer. So, it’s not a data center, right, when you think about some of what you’re reading in the news on a day-to-day basis about a data center. This is three racks. It fit within the existing power load of our on-base data, small data center. It is a liquid cooled (closed-loop) computer, so it’s not consuming water from local wells or sources. But it is a very powerful, the state-of-the-art supercomputer that can handle up to 27 trillion parameter models, which is enough to handle any of the frontier models or develop state-of-the art models from machine learning to large language models and everything in between.

Terry Gerton I know NPS’s curriculum has a lot of technology in it, and naval programs are very technology-based, but what made NVIDIA want to drop those three racks at Naval Postgraduate School? What is the incentive there?
Mike Owen Well, the Naval Postgraduate School has a long history in high-performance compute. This is not the first time that a technology giant, if you will, has seen the need to partner, the impetus to partner with the Naval Postgraduate school. In January of 1960, the very first transistor supercomputer by Seymour Craig was installed personally here on base. Which led to the Navy moving their modeling and ocean modeling command to Monterey from Annapolis about a year later. So there’s a long history of high-performance computing here, of computer science. It is a STEM, the Navy and Marine Corps STEM university. But we also have a long-history in operations research, which is optimization, analysis through data. And so in a lot of ways, Naval Postgraduate School has been at the forefront of operations research. And so those two areas, I always say three areas, right? Computer science, operations research and optimization, meteorology, and oceanography are three areas that we’re working initially in with this supercomputer. But I think it wasn’t actually the technology and the history of the research that I think was most interesting to Jensen Huang when he sat next to Adam Rwando at a meeting in Silicon Valley in the fall of 2024. It was actually our students, you know, as we have at any one time, 1300 to 1400, a mid-career officers of all services, we have allied and partner students here from about 40 different countries at any time. And all of these folks bring with them direct experience from the field, you now, from a float tours, operational tours. So that is what led to the initial framing, which was a cooperative research and development agreement with Nvidia. Shortly after that initial conversation in ’24. And then it took a while from Jensen speaking it, I wanna give you this supercomputer to work through the processes to accept a gift of that magnitude through the secretary of the Navy, but then also it was not trivial to actually install it onto the base. So it did take about, I guess about 18 months from kind of, I wanna do this. To when we had the ribbon cutting on July 22nd with him and Admiral Paparo, the PACOM commander here on the NPS campus.
Terry Gerton Captain Mike Owen is the vice provost for Warfare Studies and the leader of the NPS AI Task Force at the Naval Postgraduate School. I want to come back to the capacity of the computer in a second, but first I want to just follow on the donation process because it’s pretty unusual to have a gift of this size done through the Defense Department. And it was a donation through the NPS Foundation, given that it wasn’t a procurement. What kind of guardrails now govern the relationship between Naval Postgraduate School and NVIDIA?
Mike Owen Sure, well, as I mentioned earlier, this was part of a cooperative research and development agreement, right? Which is a mechanism by which the Department of War and industry can establish a relationship that protects IP on both sides, it governs what can and can’t happen. There is not, in this case, the cooperative research and development agreement is not a, it doesn’t come with direct money to the school. But it does come, what we do have on base is a, what NVIDIA refers to is an AI tech center, which is actually an NVIDIA solution architect, an actual person who’s on campus with us, five days a week, his full-time job is here to help our faculty and students optimize usage of the AI, the NVIDA architecture that has come through the donation. And I want to be clear, it wasn’t just NVIDIA. It was several other companies in NVIDIA’s ecosystem that presented VAST was one of the other companies, DDN for storage. So VAST had provided the cooling, DDN, the storage. So there were multiple companies who came together. Although NVIDIA gets the big headlines often, they have a very large ecosystem that they work with in partnership.
Terry Gerton Thanks for explaining that. And now that you have the three racks on board and operational, what kinds of research questions does this open up for the students at NPS?
Mike Owen Great question. So one of the things that we’re gonna do in the ocean, the oceanography realm, really in the acoustic realm, one of our faculty members is going to develop the world’s largest passive ocean acoustic neural networks. This is a very niche area. There’s not a huge industry drive to model the ocean in this way. If you think about, I think everybody’s seen the visual discriminator models where I can, is it a cat or a dog, right? You get the images that pop up and you select all the boxes that have stoplights in it. Well, that is a very relatively simple model that can discriminate between a cat and a dog. Well, if you’re talking about ocean acoustics and you want to understand, is that shrimp? Is that tectonics? Is that a whale, is that a surface ship? Is that a submarine? Is that an airplane flying overhead? All those things can manifest themselves in the acoustic environment and it’s a much more complex problem to solve, but one that’s of great importance when you’re trying to determine where an enemy submarine is, for instance, acoustically. So that’s one of the areas that we’ll be working in. Also in defensive cyberspace. Operations, that field of cyber is becoming much more prevalent on a daily basis. We see it in the news with potential cyber attacks against our infrastructure. Water plants has been the most recent news regarding cyber, and so being able to leverage this compute capability to develop new and novel techniques to identify where adversaries are on networks and then to develop options to eliminate them off of the network.
Terry Gerton It’s pretty clear that those problems require some robust computing on the back end to get to answers. What about the general student population? Will they have much interaction with this, or how are they responding to the spread of AI probably through the curriculum?
Mike Owen So the average non-computer science, non-operations research student probably wouldn’t leverage the GB300 because it is such a powerful, powerful computer. But there are other opportunities for them. We have other high-performance compute that’s not quite at the scale of this new NVIDIA DGX GB300. But we’ve also added in an AI literacy component for our students, which is a set of 10, about 40 minute lectures given by our faculty across multiple departments. They’re really the the undergirding context that any military leader needs to understand about how AI tools work. There’s a lot of information about generative AI or large language models, but that’s just one aspect of artificial intelligence and machine learning capabilities. There is autonomy, there are neural networks, there’s computer vision, all of these have military application and context, and each have their associated weaknesses and risks. And so our leaders need to understand those risks when they’re looking to employ these tools as they come into the fleet and force. Technology alone does not create advantage. Advantage is created when capable people can evaluate, integrate, employ, and sustain new capabilities in support of operational objectives. So, to this end, we have taken that AI literacy component for our students and we’re making it available to the entire Department of War via the Joint Knowledge Online platform so that commands and leadership can offer that training and education to their people, but also to track completion, which removes the administrative burden of trying to manage other methodologies.
Terry Gerton is host of the Federal Drive and has been working in or with the federal government for more than 40 years.
